Additive, beta and selection regression tables

Source: vignettes/articles/table-regression-additive.Rmd
table-regression-additive.Rmd
library(spicy)
library(mgcv)            # gam(), bam()
library(betareg)         # betareg()
library(sampleSelection) # selection(), heckit(), treatReg()

This article covers three kinds of models that estimate something beside their regression coefficients: the smooth terms of a generalized additive model, the precision submodel of a beta regression, and the error terms of a sample-selection model. table_regression() shows each of them in a labeled block of rows under the coefficients. The companion article Publication-ready regression tables covers the shared mechanics (output engines, labels, tidy()), and the class-by-class map is Supported models.

Generalized additive models

A generalized additive model replaces the straight line of a predictor by a curve estimated from the data. The example is the one of Regression tables for rms fits: diabetes among 532 women of Pima heritage aged 21 or more (MASS::Pima.tr and Pima.te), and the shape of its relation with age. The first model is linear in age. The second gives age a smooth term.

pima <- rbind(MASS::Pima.tr, MASS::Pima.te)
fit_glm <- glm(type ~ age + bmi + glu + npreg, family = binomial,
               data = pima)
fit_gam <- gam(type ~ s(age) + bmi + glu + npreg, family = binomial,
               data = pima, method = "REML")
table_regression(list(Linear = fit_glm, GAM = fit_gam))
#> Regression comparison: type
#> 
#>                              Linear                 GAM         
#>                        ───────────────────  ─────────────────── 
#>  Variable            │   B      SE     p      B      SE     p   
#> ─────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept)         │  -9.34  0.87  <.001   -8.13  0.84  <.001 
#>  age                 │   0.03  0.01   .044                      
#>  bmi                 │   0.09  0.02  <.001    0.08  0.02  <.001 
#>  glu                 │   0.04  0.00  <.001    0.04  0.00  <.001 
#>  npreg               │   0.11  0.04   .008    0.05  0.05   .244 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Smooth terms (edf): │                                          
#>    s(age)            │                        3.63   –     .002 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n                   │ 532                  532                 
#>  R² (Tjur)           │   0.34                 0.36              
#>  R² (McFadden)       │   0.29                 0.32              
#>  AIC                 │ 491.1                479.2               
#> 
#> Note. Linear: logistic regression; GAM: logistic GAM. Std. errors: Linear: classical (Fisher information), GAM: Bayesian (posterior covariance). Smooth terms: effective degrees of freedom (edf) and approximate test of each term. AIC = Akaike information criterion.
summary(fit_gam)$s.table
#>             edf   Ref.df   Chi.sq     p-value
#> s(age) 3.630771 4.561711 19.24352 0.001747507

A curve has no single coefficient, so s(age) has no row among the coefficients. It has a row in the Smooth terms (edf) block, and what stands in the B column there is the number of effective degrees of freedom of the term. One degree of freedom is a straight line. The curve of age takes 3.63, the value of summary().

The p-value of that row belongs to the test that the term is zero. mgcv computes it, and its help says what it is worth: “Be warned, these are only approximate” (?summary.gam). The standard error and the interval have no meaning for a number of degrees of freedom and stay empty.

The standard errors of the two columns do not come from the same place, and the note says so. Those of the GAM are taken from the Bayesian posterior covariance matrix of mgcv, as in its summary().

Is the effect of age linear?

The linear model is the additive model whose curve is a line. The two can be compared, and nested = TRUE adds the test to the table.

table_regression(list(Linear = fit_glm, GAM = fit_gam), nested = TRUE)
#> Hierarchical regression: type
#> 
#>                              Linear                    GAM            
#>                        ───────────────────  ───────────────────────── 
#>  Variable            │   B      SE     p         B         SE     p   
#> ─────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept)         │  -9.34  0.87  <.001   -8.13        0.84  <.001 
#>  age                 │   0.03  0.01   .044                            
#>  bmi                 │   0.09  0.02  <.001    0.08        0.02  <.001 
#>  glu                 │   0.04  0.00  <.001    0.04        0.00  <.001 
#>  npreg               │   0.11  0.04   .008    0.05        0.05   .244 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Smooth terms (edf): │                                                
#>    s(age)            │                        3.63         –     .002 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n                   │ 532                  532                       
#>  R² (Tjur)           │   0.34                 0.36                    
#>  R² (McFadden)       │   0.29                 0.32                    
#>  AIC                 │ 491.1                479.2                     
#>  Δχ²                 │    –                  19.01 (2.6)              
#>  p (change)          │    –                   <.001                   
#> 
#> Note. Linear: logistic regression; GAM: logistic GAM. Std. errors: Linear: classical (Fisher information), GAM: Bayesian (posterior covariance). Change test of an additive model: approximate, on the difference in effective degrees of freedom. Smooth terms: effective degrees of freedom (edf) and approximate test of each term. AIC = Akaike information criterion.
anova(fit_glm, fit_gam, test = "Chisq")
#> Analysis of Deviance Table
#> 
#> Model 1: type ~ age + bmi + glu + npreg
#> Model 2: type ~ s(age) + bmi + glu + npreg
#>   Resid. Df Resid. Dev     Df Deviance  Pr(>Chi)    
#> 1    527.00     481.12                              
#> 2    524.37     462.11 2.6308   19.006 0.0001749 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

The deviance falls by 19.01 for 2.6 more effective degrees of freedom, p < .001: the relation with age is not a line. The numbers are those of anova(). The degrees of freedom are not whole, since the test takes the difference in effective degrees of freedom of the two models, and the note recalls that the test is approximate. The help of mgcv says that these p-values “must be used with care” (?anova.gam).

Several smooth terms

A model can be made of smooth terms only. Each has its row.

fit_gam3 <- gam(type ~ s(age) + s(glu) + te(bmi, ped), family = binomial,
                data = pima, method = "REML")
table_regression(fit_gam3)
#> Logistic GAM: type
#> 
#>  Variable            │   B      SE       95% CI        p   
#> ─────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept)         │  -1.09  0.14  [-1.36, -0.83]  <.001 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Smooth terms (edf): │                                     
#>    s(age)            │   3.54   –          –         <.001 
#>    s(glu)            │   1.00   –          –         <.001 
#>    te(bmi,ped)       │   8.21   –          –         <.001 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n                   │ 532                                 
#>  R² (Tjur)           │   0.40                              
#>  R² (McFadden)       │   0.36                              
#>  AIC                 │ 465.7                               
#> 
#> Note. Logistic GAM. Std. errors: Bayesian (posterior covariance). Smooth terms: effective degrees of freedom (edf) and approximate test of each term. CI = confidence interval; AIC = Akaike information criterion.
summary(fit_gam3)$s.table
#>                  edf    Ref.df   Chi.sq      p-value
#> s(age)      3.544690  4.444677 37.53214 5.616457e-07
#> s(glu)      1.000150  1.000299 64.78000 0.000000e+00
#> te(bmi,ped) 8.209722 10.422729 41.38410 1.621210e-05

The smooth of glucose has 1.00 effective degree of freedom: the penalty has brought it back to a straight line. te(bmi, ped) is a surface in two predictors, with 8.21.

Selecting and labeling rows

The smooth terms are predictors, and keep, drop and labels treat them as such, under the name mgcv gives them.

table_regression(fit_gam, drop = "^s\\(")
#> Logistic GAM: type
#> 
#>  Variable      │   B      SE       95% CI        p   
#> ───────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept)   │  -8.13  0.84  [-9.77, -6.49]  <.001 
#>  bmi           │   0.08  0.02  [ 0.04,  0.11]  <.001 
#>  glu           │   0.04  0.00  [ 0.03,  0.04]  <.001 
#>  npreg         │   0.05  0.05  [-0.04,  0.14]   .244 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n             │ 532                                 
#>  R² (Tjur)     │   0.36                              
#>  R² (McFadden) │   0.32                              
#>  AIC           │ 479.2                               
#> 
#> Note. Logistic GAM. Std. errors: Bayesian (posterior covariance). CI = confidence interval; AIC = Akaike information criterion.
table_regression(fit_gam, keep = "s(age)")
#> Logistic GAM: type
#> 
#>  Variable            │   B      SE       95% CI        p   
#> ─────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept)         │  -8.13  0.84  [-9.77, -6.49]  <.001 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Smooth terms (edf): │                                     
#>    s(age)            │   3.63   –          –          .002 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n                   │ 532                                 
#>  R² (Tjur)           │   0.36                              
#>  R² (McFadden)       │   0.32                              
#>  AIC                 │ 479.2                               
#> 
#> Note. Logistic GAM. Std. errors: Bayesian (posterior covariance). Smooth terms: effective degrees of freedom (edf) and approximate test of each term. CI = confidence interval; AIC = Akaike information criterion.
table_regression(fit_gam, labels = c("s(age)" = "Age (smooth)"))
#> Logistic GAM: type
#> 
#>  Variable            │   B      SE       95% CI        p   
#> ─────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept)         │  -8.13  0.84  [-9.77, -6.49]  <.001 
#>  bmi                 │   0.08  0.02  [ 0.04,  0.11]  <.001 
#>  glu                 │   0.04  0.00  [ 0.03,  0.04]  <.001 
#>  npreg               │   0.05  0.05  [-0.04,  0.14]   .244 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Smooth terms (edf): │                                     
#>    Age (smooth)      │   3.63   –          –          .002 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n                   │ 532                                 
#>  R² (Tjur)           │   0.36                              
#>  R² (McFadden)       │   0.32                              
#>  AIC                 │ 479.2                               
#> 
#> Note. Logistic GAM. Std. errors: Bayesian (posterior covariance). Smooth terms: effective degrees of freedom (edf) and approximate test of each term. CI = confidence interval; AIC = Akaike information criterion.

drop and keep take regular expressions, and also the exact name of a term, written as it is: "s(age)" needs no escaping. When no smooth row is left, the block and its sentence in the note are left out.

Cluster-robust variance

vcov = "CR1" with a cluster gives the parametric rows a sandwich variance. These data have no cluster, and the number of pregnancies stands in for one here, only to show what the table does.

table_regression(fit_gam, vcov = "CR1", cluster = ~npreg)
#> Logistic GAM: type
#> 
#>  Variable            │   B      SE       95% CI        p   
#> ─────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept)         │  -8.13  0.78  [-9.65, -6.61]  <.001 
#>  bmi                 │   0.08  0.02  [ 0.04,  0.12]  <.001 
#>  glu                 │   0.04  0.00  [ 0.03,  0.04]  <.001 
#>  npreg               │   0.05  0.05  [-0.04,  0.14]   .240 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Smooth terms (edf): │                                     
#>    s(age)            │   3.63   –          –          –    
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n                   │ 532                                 
#>  R² (Tjur)           │   0.36                              
#>  R² (McFadden)       │   0.32                              
#>  AIC                 │ 479.2                               
#> 
#> Note. Logistic GAM. Std. errors: cluster-robust (CR1), clusters by npreg. Smooth terms: effective degrees of freedom (edf). The test of the smooth terms is not computed under a robust variance. CI = confidence interval; AIC = Akaike information criterion.

The test of a smooth term rests on the covariance matrix of mgcv. It is not computed under a robust variance: the row keeps its degrees of freedom, and its p-value is empty.

Average marginal effects

The table has given age a shape and a test, and no direction yet. The average marginal effect does: it is the slope of the predicted probability with respect to age, averaged over the sample.

table_regression(fit_gam, show_columns = c("b", "p", "ame", "ame_p"))
#> Logistic GAM: type
#> 
#>  Variable            │   B       p    AME     p   
#> ─────────────────────┼────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept)         │  -8.13  <.001              
#>  bmi                 │   0.08  <.001  0.01  <.001 
#>  glu                 │   0.04  <.001  0.01  <.001 
#>  npreg               │   0.05   .244  0.01   .242 
#>  age                 │                0.01  <.001 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Smooth terms (edf): │                            
#>    s(age)            │   3.63   .002              
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n                   │ 532                        
#>  R² (Tjur)           │   0.36                     
#>  R² (McFadden)       │   0.32                     
#>  AIC                 │ 479.2                      
#> 
#> Note. Logistic GAM. Std. errors: Bayesian (posterior covariance). AME of a continuous predictor: average slope (dY/dX). Smooth terms: effective degrees of freedom (edf) and approximate test of each term. AME = average marginal effect; AIC = Akaike information criterion.

One more year of age goes with a probability of diabetes higher by about one percentage point on average. The row of age comes after the parametric terms, with an empty B, since the curve has no coefficient. The p-value that follows the AME column is that of the AME.

The long format

tidy() returns the smooth rows with estimate_type = "edf". The reference degrees of freedom are in df, the test in statistic and p.value.

td <- broom::tidy(table_regression(fit_gam))
td[, c("term", "estimate_type", "estimate", "df", "statistic", "p.value")]
#> # A tibble: 5 × 6
#>   term        estimate_type estimate     df statistic  p.value
#>   <chr>       <chr>            <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 (Intercept) B              -8.13   Inf        -9.71 2.85e-22
#> 2 bmi         B               0.0796 Inf         4.41 1.05e- 5
#> 3 glu         B               0.0354 Inf         8.51 1.79e-17
#> 4 npreg       B               0.0532 Inf         1.16 2.44e- 1
#> 5 s(age)      edf             3.63     4.56     19.2  1.75e- 3

Large data: bam()

bam() fits the same models on large data. The example takes the 28,155 men of AER::CPS1988 and the logarithm of their wage, with a smooth of experience.

data("CPS1988", package = "AER")
fit_bam <- bam(log(wage) ~ s(experience) + education + ethnicity + smsa +
                 region + parttime, data = CPS1988)
table_regression(fit_bam)
#> Generalized additive model (GAM): log(wage)
#> 
#>  Variable            │    B       SE       95% CI        p   
#> ─────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept)         │     5.07  0.02  [ 5.04,  5.11]  <.001 
#>  education           │     0.09  0.00  [ 0.08,  0.09]  <.001 
#>  ethnicity:          │                                       
#>    cauc (ref.)       │      –     –          –          –    
#>    afam              │    -0.23  0.01  [-0.25, -0.21]  <.001 
#>  smsa:               │                                       
#>    no (ref.)         │      –     –          –          –    
#>    yes               │     0.16  0.01  [ 0.15,  0.18]  <.001 
#>  region:             │                                       
#>    northeast (ref.)  │      –     –          –          –    
#>    midwest           │    -0.05  0.01  [-0.07, -0.03]  <.001 
#>    south             │    -0.10  0.01  [-0.12, -0.08]  <.001 
#>    west              │    -0.05  0.01  [-0.06, -0.03]  <.001 
#>  parttime:           │                                       
#>    no (ref.)         │      –     –          –          –    
#>    yes               │    -0.84  0.01  [-0.87, -0.82]  <.001 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Smooth terms (edf): │                                       
#>    s(experience)     │     8.19   –          –         <.001 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n                   │ 28155                                 
#>  R² (deviance)       │     0.46                              
#>  AIC                 │ 43582.2                               
#> 
#> Note. Generalized additive model (GAM). Std. errors: Bayesian (posterior covariance). Smooth terms: effective degrees of freedom (edf) and approximate test of each term. CI = confidence interval; AIC = Akaike information criterion.
summary(fit_bam)$s.table
#>                    edf   Ref.df        F p-value
#> s(experience) 8.188189 8.693827 837.2108       0

The table reads like that of gam(). The title keeps the outcome as the formula writes it, log(wage). For a Gaussian model the test of a smooth term is an F test, and the fit statistic is the R² of the deviance.

What is refused

gamm() estimates an additive model as a mixed model and returns two parts, lme and gam. Neither is read, and the error says why.

fit_gamm <- gamm(glu ~ s(age) + bmi, data = pima)
table_regression(fit_gamm$gam)
#> Error in `table_regression()`:
#> ! The `gam` part of a `mgcv::gamm()` fit is not supported by `table_regression()`.
#> ℹ Its standard errors come from the mixed model of the `lme` part, and its likelihood and information criteria are not those of the model.
#> ℹ Fit the model with `mgcv::gam()`, a random intercept written as `s(g, bs = "re")`, which is supported, or report `summary(fit$gam)`.

Beta regression

A beta regression is a model for a proportion that stays strictly between 0 and 1. The example is the one of Ferrari and Cribari-Neto (2004): the share of income that 38 households spend on food (betareg::FoodExpenditure), by income and by number of persons in the household.

The model has two parameters. The mean of the share depends on the predictors through a link, the logit by default. The precision φ says how tightly the shares gather around that mean: for a given mean, a larger φ is a smaller variance. The first model below holds the precision constant. The second lets it depend on the size of the household, with the formula y ~ x | z. The coefficient of income is small, and the tables of this section show three decimals.

data("FoodExpenditure", package = "betareg")
FoodExpenditure$share <- FoodExpenditure$food / FoodExpenditure$income
fit_beta  <- betareg(share ~ income + persons, data = FoodExpenditure)
fit_beta2 <- betareg(share ~ income + persons | persons,
                     data = FoodExpenditure)
table_regression(list("Constant precision" = fit_beta,
                      "Precision ~ persons" = fit_beta2), digits = 3)
#> Beta regression comparison: share
#> 
#>                   Constant precision     Precision ~ persons  
#>                  ─────────────────────  ───────────────────── 
#>  Variable      │    B      SE      p       B      SE      p   
#> ───────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept)   │  -0.623  0.224   .005   -0.783  0.178  <.001 
#>  income        │  -0.012  0.003  <.001   -0.008  0.002  <.001 
#>  persons       │   0.118  0.035  <.001    0.093  0.035   .008 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Precision:    │                                              
#>    (Intercept) │                          5.504  0.533  <.001 
#>    persons     │                         -0.484  0.133  <.001 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n             │  38                     38                   
#>  AIC           │ -82.7                  -88.4                 
#> 
#> Note. Beta regression models. Std. errors: classical (Fisher information). Precision component: log scale. AIC = Akaike information criterion.

The coefficients of the first column are those of Table 2 of Ferrari and Cribari-Neto. In the second, the submodel of the precision has its own block, Precision, with a coefficient, a standard error and a test for each of its terms. They are on the scale of the link of the precision, the logarithm. The coefficient of persons is negative: the shares of the larger households are more dispersed.

summary() gives the same numbers.

summary(fit_beta)$coefficients
#> $mean
#>                Estimate  Std. Error   z value     Pr(>|z|)
#> (Intercept) -0.62254806 0.223853539 -2.781051 5.418326e-03
#> income      -0.01229884 0.003035585 -4.051556 5.087819e-05
#> persons      0.11846210 0.035340667  3.352005 8.022853e-04
#> 
#> $precision
#>       Estimate Std. Error  z value     Pr(>|z|)
#> (phi) 35.60975   8.079598 4.407366 1.046351e-05
summary(fit_beta2)$coefficients
#> $mean
#>                 Estimate  Std. Error   z value     Pr(>|z|)
#> (Intercept) -0.783081551 0.177708226 -4.406558 1.050263e-05
#> income      -0.008216837 0.002410524 -3.408734 6.526502e-04
#> persons      0.092553806 0.034821371  2.657960 7.861526e-03
#> 
#> $precision
#>               Estimate Std. Error   z value     Pr(>|z|)
#> (Intercept)  5.5043097  0.5333500 10.320258 5.706974e-25
#> persons     -0.4835233  0.1334643 -3.622866 2.913567e-04

A constant precision is one number, and it has no block: it is the "phi" fit statistic, shown below.

The mean submodel alone

show_components = FALSE leaves the block out.

table_regression(fit_beta2, show_components = FALSE, digits = 3)
#> Beta regression: share
#> 
#>  Variable    │    B      SE         95% CI         p   
#> ─────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept) │  -0.783  0.178  [-1.131, -0.435]  <.001 
#>  income      │  -0.008  0.002  [-0.013, -0.003]  <.001 
#>  persons     │   0.093  0.035  [ 0.024,  0.161]   .008 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n           │  38                                     
#>  AIC         │ -88.4                                   
#> 
#> Note. Beta regression. Std. errors: classical (Fisher information). CI = confidence interval; AIC = Akaike information criterion.

Odds ratios

With the logit link, a coefficient of the mean submodel is a log odds ratio of the expected proportion, and exponentiate = TRUE shows the odds ratio.

table_regression(fit_beta2, exponentiate = TRUE, digits = 3)
#> Beta regression: share
#> 
#>  Variable      │   OR      SE         95% CI         p   
#> ───────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept)   │   0.457  0.081  [ 0.323,  0.647]  <.001 
#>  income        │   0.992  0.002  [ 0.987,  0.997]  <.001 
#>  persons       │   1.097  0.038  [ 1.025,  1.174]   .008 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Precision:    │                                         
#>    (Intercept) │   5.504  0.533  [ 4.459,  6.550]  <.001 
#>    persons     │  -0.484  0.133  [-0.745, -0.222]  <.001 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n             │  38                                     
#>  AIC           │ -88.4                                   
#> 
#> Note. Beta regression. Coefficients exponentiated and displayed as OR; SE on the OR scale (delta method); CI bounds exponentiated (asymmetric). The (Intercept) row estimates the baseline odds. Std. errors: classical (Fisher information). Precision component: log scale. The component rows stay on the link scale (not exponentiated). CI = confidence interval; AIC = Akaike information criterion.

One more person in the household multiplies the odds of the expected food share by 1.10, 95% CI [1.02, 1.17]. The precision block is not exponentiated: its coefficients are not log odds, and its rows stay on the scale of their link.

Other links and fit statistics

betareg() takes other links for the mean. The note names a link other than the logit, and so does the title of a table of one model.

fit_probit <- update(fit_beta, link = "probit")
table_regression(list(Logit = fit_beta, Probit = fit_probit), digits = 3,
                 show_fit_stats = c("nobs", "phi", "pseudo_r2_ferrari", "aic"))
#> Beta regression comparison: share
#> 
#>                                        Logit                 Probit         
#>                                ─────────────────────  ───────────────────── 
#>  Variable                    │    B      SE      p       B      SE      p   
#> ─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept)                 │  -0.623  0.224   .005   -0.389  0.136   .004 
#>  income                      │  -0.012  0.003  <.001   -0.007  0.002  <.001 
#>  persons                     │   0.118  0.035  <.001    0.070  0.021   .001 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n                           │  38                     38                   
#>  φ (precision)               │  35.61                  35.13                
#>  R² (Ferrari & Cribari-Neto) │   0.39                   0.40                
#>  AIC                         │ -82.7                  -82.2                 
#> 
#> Note. Logit: beta regression; Probit: probit beta regression. Std. errors: classical (Fisher information). AIC = Akaike information criterion.
table_regression(fit_probit, digits = 3)
#> Probit beta regression: share
#> 
#>  Variable    │    B      SE         95% CI         p   
#> ─────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept) │  -0.389  0.136  [-0.655, -0.123]   .004 
#>  income      │  -0.007  0.002  [-0.011, -0.004]  <.001 
#>  persons     │   0.070  0.021  [ 0.028,  0.111]   .001 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n           │  38                                     
#>  AIC         │ -82.2                                   
#> 
#> Note. Probit beta regression. Std. errors: classical (Fisher information). CI = confidence interval; AIC = Akaike information criterion.
c(logit = fit_beta$pseudo.r.squared, probit = fit_probit$pseudo.r.squared)
#>     logit    probit 
#> 0.3878327 0.3989190

Two fit statistics are specific to these models. "phi" is the constant precision. "pseudo_r2_ferrari" is the pseudo-R² that summary() prints, the squared correlation between the linear predictor and the outcome on the scale of the link. Neither is in the default rows, which are the number of observations and the AIC.

Does the precision vary?

The two models of the first table are nested, and nested = TRUE tests the precision submodel by a likelihood-ratio test.

table_regression(list("Constant precision" = fit_beta,
                      "Precision ~ persons" = fit_beta2),
                 nested = TRUE, digits = 3)
#> Hierarchical beta regression: share
#> 
#>                   Constant precision       Precision ~ persons    
#>                  ─────────────────────  ───────────────────────── 
#>  Variable      │    B      SE      p         B        SE      p   
#> ───────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept)   │  -0.623  0.224   .005   -0.783      0.178  <.001 
#>  income        │  -0.012  0.003  <.001   -0.008      0.002  <.001 
#>  persons       │   0.118  0.035  <.001    0.093      0.035   .008 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Precision:    │                                                  
#>    (Intercept) │                          5.504      0.533  <.001 
#>    persons     │                         -0.484      0.133  <.001 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n             │  38                     38                       
#>  AIC           │ -82.7                  -88.4                     
#>  Δχ²           │    –                     7.703 (1)               
#>  p (change)    │    –                      .006                   
#> 
#> Note. Beta regression models. Std. errors: classical (Fisher information). Precision component: log scale. AIC = Akaike information criterion.
lmtest::lrtest(fit_beta, fit_beta2)
#> Likelihood ratio test
#> 
#> Model 1: share ~ income + persons
#> Model 2: share ~ income + persons | persons
#>   #Df LogLik Df  Chisq Pr(>Chisq)   
#> 1   4 45.334                        
#> 2   5 49.185  1 7.7029   0.005513 **
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

The test is that of lmtest::lrtest(): 7.70 on 1 degree of freedom, p = .006. The precision depends on the size of the household.

Effects on the proportion

Coefficients on the logit scale do not say by how much the share changes. The average marginal effects do, on the scale of the proportion.

table_regression(fit_beta2, show_columns = c("b", "p", "ame", "ame_p"),
                 digits = 4)
#> Beta regression: share
#> 
#>  Variable      │    B        p      AME      p   
#> ───────────────┼─────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept)   │  -0.7831  <.001                 
#>  income        │  -0.0082  <.001  -0.0017  <.001 
#>  persons       │   0.0926   .008   0.0187   .010 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Precision:    │                                 
#>    (Intercept) │   5.5043  <.001                 
#>    persons     │  -0.4835  <.001                 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n             │  38                             
#>  AIC           │ -88.4                           
#> 
#> Note. Beta regression. Std. errors: classical (Fisher information). AME of a continuous predictor: average slope (dY/dX). Precision component: log scale. AME = average marginal effect; AIC = Akaike information criterion.

One more person goes with an expected food share higher by 1.9 percentage points on average. The precision block has no AME: the effects are those of the mean submodel.

Sample-selection models

A sample-selection model has two equations. The first, a probit, says who is observed. The second is the regression of interest, estimated on those who are. The two error terms may be correlated, and the model estimates that correlation. The example is the one of the help of selection(): the wage of 753 married women (Mroz87), of whom 428 were in the labor force and have a wage.

selection() estimates the model by maximum likelihood, heckit() by the two-step method. Family income is counted in thousands of dollars here, and the tables show three decimals.

data("Mroz87", package = "sampleSelection")
Mroz87$kids <- Mroz87$kids5 + Mroz87$kids618 > 0
Mroz87$faminc <- Mroz87$faminc / 1000
fit_ml <- selection(lfp ~ age + I(age^2) + faminc + kids + educ,
                    wage ~ exper + I(exper^2) + educ + city, data = Mroz87)
fit_2s <- heckit(lfp ~ age + I(age^2) + faminc + kids + educ,
                 wage ~ exper + I(exper^2) + educ + city, data = Mroz87)
table_regression(fit_ml, digits = 3)
#> Heckman selection model: wage
#> 
#>                                   Outcome               Selection       
#>                            ──────────────────────  ──────────────────── 
#>  Variable                │    B       SE      p      B      SE      p   
#> ─────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept)             │   -1.963  1.198   .102  -4.120  1.401   .003 
#>  exper                   │    0.028  0.062   .651                       
#>  I(exper^2)              │   -0.000  0.002   .955                       
#>  educ                    │    0.457  0.073  <.001   0.095  0.023  <.001 
#>  city                    │    0.447  0.316   .158                       
#>  age                     │                          0.184  0.066   .005 
#>  I(age^2)                │                         -0.002  0.001   .002 
#>  faminc                  │                          0.006  0.004   .199 
#>  kids:                   │                                              
#>    FALSE (ref.)          │                           –      –      –    
#>    TRUE                  │                         -0.451  0.130  <.001 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Error terms:            │                                              
#>    σ (outcome error)     │    3.108  0.114   –                          
#>    ρ (error correlation) │   -0.132  0.165   .424                       
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n                       │  753                                         
#>  AIC                     │ 3188.5                                       
#> 
#> Note. Heckman selection model. Outcome observed for 428 of 753. Std. errors: classical (Fisher information). P-values and CIs: t distribution with 740 df. Error terms: σ, standard deviation of the outcome error; ρ, correlation of the selection and outcome errors. AIC = Akaike information criterion.

A model alone sets its two equations side by side: the wage equation under Outcome, then the probit of participation under Selection. A variable fills the cells of the equations it enters. Education is in the two: it raises the probability of working and, among the women who work, the wage. kids is a logical variable and has a row for each of its values, the reference first. outcome_labels renames the two groups.

The Error terms block holds what the model estimates beside its coefficients, and the note defines each of them. σ is the standard deviation of the error of the wage equation. ρ is the correlation between the errors of the two equations. If it is zero, the women who work are not selected on what the model does not observe, and a regression on them alone would do. Here ρ is −0.13, p = .424: these data give no sign of such a selection.

Beside another selection model, the equations go back to rows, which set the two estimators of a coefficient on one line: each variable has a selection row, an outcome row, or both.

table_regression(list(Likelihood = fit_ml, Heckit = fit_2s), digits = 3)
#> Heckman selection model comparison: wage
#> 
#>                                    Likelihood               Heckit         
#>                              ──────────────────────  ───────────────────── 
#>  Variable                  │    B       SE      p       B      SE      p   
#> ───────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept):              │                                               
#>    selection               │   -4.120  1.401   .003   -4.157  1.402   .003 
#>    outcome                 │   -1.963  1.198   .102   -0.971  2.059   .637 
#>  age:                      │                                               
#>    selection               │    0.184  0.066   .005    0.185  0.066   .005 
#>  I(age^2):                 │                                               
#>    selection               │   -0.002  0.001   .002   -0.002  0.001   .002 
#>  faminc:                   │                                               
#>    selection               │    0.006  0.004   .199    0.005  0.004   .277 
#>  kids:                     │                                               
#>    selection: FALSE (ref.) │     –      –      –        –      –      –    
#>    selection: TRUE         │   -0.451  0.130  <.001   -0.449  0.131  <.001 
#>  educ:                     │                                               
#>    selection               │    0.095  0.023  <.001    0.098  0.023  <.001 
#>    outcome                 │    0.457  0.073  <.001    0.417  0.100  <.001 
#>  exper:                    │                                               
#>    outcome                 │    0.028  0.062   .651    0.021  0.062   .736 
#>  I(exper^2):               │                                               
#>    outcome                 │   -0.000  0.002   .955    0.000  0.002   .942 
#>  city:                     │                                               
#>    outcome                 │    0.447  0.316   .158    0.444  0.316   .160 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Error terms:              │                                               
#>    σ (outcome error)       │    3.108  0.114   –       3.200   –      –    
#>    λ (inverse Mills ratio) │                          -1.098  1.266   .386 
#>    ρ (error correlation)   │   -0.132  0.165   .424   -0.343   –      –    
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n                         │  753                    753                   
#>  AIC                       │ 3188.5                     –                  
#> 
#> Note. Heckman selection models. Outcome observed for 428 of 753. Std. errors: Likelihood: classical (Fisher information), Heckit: classical (two-step). P-values and CIs: t distribution with 740 df. Error terms: λ, coefficient of the inverse Mills ratio, an estimate of ρσ; σ, standard deviation of the outcome error; ρ, correlation of the selection and outcome errors. In a two-step fit, σ and ρ are derived from the estimates and have no standard error. AIC = Akaike information criterion.

The two-step method does not estimate ρ directly. It adds a regressor to the wage equation, the inverse Mills ratio, whose coefficient λ estimates ρσ, and it is the test of λ that plays this role (p = .386). σ and ρ are then derived from the estimates, without a standard error. A two-step fit has no likelihood, hence no AIC.

The note also gives the number of observations whose outcome is observed, the standard errors of each model, and the reference distribution of the tests. summary() reports the same values.

summary(fit_ml)$estimate[c("educ", "sigma", "rho"), ]
#>         Estimate Std. Error    t value      Pr(>|t|)
#> educ   0.0952808 0.02315342  4.1151936  4.303375e-05
#> sigma  3.1083762 0.11383277 27.3065142 4.201283e-114
#> rho   -0.1319586 0.16512710 -0.7991335  4.244694e-01
summary(fit_2s)$estimate[c("educ", "invMillsRatio", "sigma", "rho"), ]
#>                  Estimate Std. Error    t value     Pr(>|t|)
#> educ           0.09818228 0.02298412  4.2717441 2.192529e-05
#> invMillsRatio -1.09761942 1.26598561 -0.8670078 3.862188e-01
#> sigma          3.20006428         NA         NA           NA
#> rho           -0.34299918         NA         NA           NA

The help of selection() states what these models assume: “a known (multivariate normal) distribution of error terms”. It adds that “standard errors tend to be large without a strong exclusion restriction”, that is, without a variable that enters the selection equation and not the outcome equation.

Beside least squares

A selection model is usually read against the regression it corrects. Beside a model of another class, its two equations become two groups of columns, and the rows align term by term.

fit_ols <- lm(wage ~ exper + I(exper^2) + educ + city, data = Mroz87,
              subset = lfp == 1)
table_regression(list(OLS = fit_ols, Heckman = fit_ml),
                 show_columns = c("b", "se"))
#> Regression comparison: wage
#> 
#>                                OLS       Heckman: Outcome  Heckman: Selection 
#>                            ────────────  ────────────────  ────────────────── 
#>  Variable                │   B      SE       B        SE         B        SE

#>  educ                    │   0.48  0.07      0.46    0.07       0.10     0.02 
#>  city                    │   0.45  0.32      0.45    0.32                     
#>  age                     │                                      0.18     0.07 
#>  I(age^2)                │                                     -0.00     0.00 
#>  faminc                  │                                      0.01     0.00 
#>  kids:                   │

#>    TRUE                  │                                     -0.45     0.13

#>    ρ (error correlation) │                  -0.13    0.17                     
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n                       │ 428             753

Heckman: P-values and CIs: t distribution with 740 df. Error terms: σ, standard deviation of the outcome error; ρ, correlation of the selection and outcome errors.

A year of education is worth 0.48 by least squares on the women who work and 0.46 in the outcome equation. The correction changes little here, as ρ suggested.

Comparing two selection models

Two models estimated by maximum likelihood are compared by a likelihood-ratio test.

fit_ml0 <- selection(lfp ~ age + I(age^2) + faminc + kids + educ,
                     wage ~ exper + I(exper^2) + educ, data = Mroz87)
table_regression(list("Without city" = fit_ml0, "With city" = fit_ml),
                 nested = TRUE, show_columns = c("b", "se", "p"), digits = 3)

AIC = Akaike information criterion.

Living in a city does not improve the wage equation: 1.99 on 1 degree of freedom, p = .158. The comparison is refused for a two-step fit, which has no likelihood.

A binary outcome

When the outcome is binary, its equation is a probit too, which the title and the note state, and the model has no σ.

fit_bin <- selection(lfp ~ educ + age + kids5 + kids618 + nwifeinc,
                     wage >= 5 ~ educ, data = Mroz87)
table_regression(fit_bin)
#> Heckman selection model (binary outcome): wage >= 5
#>

Treatment-effects models

treatReg() estimates the effect of a binary treatment that the units choose. The outcome is observed for everyone, and the equation under Selection is that of the treatment. The example takes the college attendance of the wife and the logarithm of the family income.

Mroz87$college <- trimws(Mroz87$wifecoll) == "TRUE"
fit_tr <- treatReg(college ~ motheduc + fatheduc + age,
                   log(faminc) ~ college + huseduc + age + city,
                   data = Mroz87)
table_regression(fit_tr)
#> Treatment-effects model: log(faminc)

Dropping an error term

The error terms are coefficients of the fit, and keep and drop select them by their name in coef(): "sigma", "rho", "invMillsRatio".

table_regression(fit_ml, drop = "sigma", show_columns = c("b", "se", "p"),
                 digits = 3)

What is refused

A tobit-5 model has two outcome equations, one for each regime. A table of one outcome cannot show it, and it is refused.

set.seed(1)
n <- 500
sim <- data.frame(z = rnorm(n), x1 = rnorm(n), x2 = rnorm(n))
e <- MASS::mvrnorm(n, c(0, 0, 0),
                   matrix(c(1, -0.5, 0.5, -0.5, 1, 0, 0.5, 0, 1), 3))
sim$s  <- sim$z + e[, 1] > 0
sim$y1 <- sim$x1 + e[, 2]
sim$y2 <- sim$x2 + e[, 3]
fit_t5 <- selection(s ~ z, list(y1 ~ x1, y2 ~ x2), data = sim)
table_regression(fit_t5)
#> Error in `table_regression()`:
#> ! A tobit-5 `selection` fit is not supported by `table_regression()`.
#> ℹ A tobit-5 (switching regression) fit has two outcome equations, one per regime; the table shows the sample-selection (tobit-2) model and the treatment-effects model of `treatReg()`.

Tables in another language

The blocks and their notes follow options(spicy.language = ).

options(spicy.language = "fr", width = 92)

The blocks are part of the table in every output engine. Here the first table as a gt object, with odds ratios.
